entry.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks

link.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks

entry.content: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

entry.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections

link.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections

entry.content: “Silicon samples” based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person’s voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.

entry.title: Statistical Inference for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent

link.title: Statistical Inference for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent

entry.content: Privacy preservation in machine learning, particularly through Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), is crucial for analyzing sensitive data. However, existing statistical inference methods for SGD predominantly focus on cyclic subsampling, while DP-SGD requires randomized subsampling. This paper first bridges this gap by establishing the asymptotic properties of SGD under the randomized rule and extending these results to DP-SGD. For DP-SGD, we show that the asymptotic variance decomposes into statistical, sampling, and privacy-induced components. We propose two methods for constructing valid confidence intervals: the plug-in method and the random scaling method. We also perform extensive numerical analysis showing that the proposed confidence intervals achieve nominal coverage rates while maintaining privacy.

entry.title: Derivative Estimation from Coarse, Irregular, Noisy Samples: An MLE-Spline Approach

link.title: Derivative Estimation from Coarse, Irregular, Noisy Samples: An MLE-Spline Approach

entry.content: We address numerical differentiation under coarse, non-uniform sampling and Gaussian noise. A maximum-likelihood estimator with $L_2$-norm constraint on a higher-order derivative is obtained, yielding spline-based solution. We introduce a non-standard parameterization of quadratic splines and develop recursive online algorithms. Two formulations—quadratic and zero-order—offer tradeoff between smoothness and computational speed. Simulations demonstrate superior performance over high-gain observers and super-twisting differentiators under coarse sampling and high noise, benefiting systems where higher sampling rates are impractical.

entry.title: Bayesian Instrumented Directed Graphical Models for Cyclic Causal Discovery with Unmeasured Confounding

link.title: Bayesian Instrumented Directed Graphical Models for Cyclic Causal Discovery with Unmeasured Confounding

entry.content: In networks with feedback, a pairwise instrumental-variable estimate can combine direct and indirect effects. We propose a Bayesian cyclic structural equation model with spike-and-slab priors on direct effects and on error covariances representing unmeasured confounding. Its joint posterior quantifies support for edges, confounding links, and feedback loops. The model has two versions. IV-RGM takes as known the map that lists which responses each instrument affects directly. IV-RGM+ learns this map. A rank condition identifies the model with a known map. For an unknown map, we give conditions on instrument effects and cycle gains that identify the representation with the fewest direct instrument effects. We establish posterior consistency and directed graph recovery under additional conditions. In smaller simulated samples with strong instruments, IV-RGM ranked direct edges more accurately than competing methods when the map was correct. When the supplied map omitted shared targets, IV-RGM+ ranked edges most accurately and reduced false discoveries relative to fixing the incorrect map. Weak instruments limited recovery across methods. In B cells, the analysis with a known map gave limited support to feedback among inhibitory receptor genes. Both versions are available in an R package on CRAN (https://cran.r-project.org/package=MR.RGM).

entry.title: Debiased Inference via Posterior Corrections for High-Dimensional Regression

link.title: Debiased Inference via Posterior Corrections for High-Dimensional Regression

entry.content: There has been significant progress in Bayesian inference based on sparsity-inducing priors, such as spike-and-slab and horseshoe priors, for high-dimensional regression. The resulting posteriors, however, in general do not possess desirable frequentist properties, and the credible sets thus cannot serve as valid confidence sets even asymptotically. We introduce a novel debiasing approach that corrects the bias for the entire (possibly approximate) Bayesian posterior distribution. We establish new Bernstein-von Mises theorems that guarantee the frequentist validity of the debiased law. We demonstrate the practical performance of our proposal through Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications in economics.

entry.title: Design-Conditional Prior Elicitation for Dirichlet Process Mixtures: A Unified Framework for Cluster Counts and Weight Control

link.title: Design-Conditional Prior Elicitation for Dirichlet Process Mixtures: A Unified Framework for Cluster Counts and Weight Control

entry.content: Dirichlet process mixtures (DPMs) model variation in effects across sites or studies and in latent traits among examinees. The concentration parameter affects both the number of clusters in the sample and the population weights, yet its hyperprior is often chosen by default. We describe a method for choosing this hyperprior when the number of units is fixed by design. We calibrate a Gamma hyperprior to the analyst’s expected cluster count and uncertainty about it, then examine the implied weights. If count and weight judgments conflict, Dual-Anchor selects a compromise and reports its implications for both. Across our simulations and applications, the choice of prior could change the inferred number of clusters considerably even when individual estimates changed little. A higher cluster count under an alternative prior warrants a closer look at the upper tail, where estimates can shift even when the median remains stable. The DPprior R package implements the calibration and diagnostics.

entry.title: BayesFlow 2: Multi-Backend Amortized Bayesian Inference in Python

link.title: BayesFlow 2: Multi-Backend Amortized Bayesian Inference in Python

entry.content: Modern Bayesian inference involves a mixture of computational methods for estimating, validating, and drawing conclusions from probabilistic models as part of principled workflows. An overarching motif of many Bayesian methods is that they are relatively slow, which often becomes prohibitive when fitting complex models to large data sets. Amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) offers a path to solving the computational challenges of Bayes. ABI trains neural networks on model simulations, rewarding users with rapid inference of any model-implied quantity, such as point estimates, likelihoods, or full posterior distributions. In this work, we present the Python library BayesFlow, Version 2, for general-purpose ABI. Along with direct posterior, likelihood, and ratio estimation, the software includes support for multiple popular deep learning backends, a rich collection of generative networks for sampling and density estimation, complete customization and high-level interfaces, as well as new capabilities for hyperparameter optimization, design optimization, and multilevel modeling. Using a case study on dynamical system parameter estimation, combined with comparisons to similar software, we show that our streamlined, user-friendly workflow has strong potential to support broad adoption.

entry.title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Predicting Donor Kidney Discard

link.title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Predicting Donor Kidney Discard

entry.content: A kidney transplant can significantly improve the life expectancy and quality of life of patients with end-stage renal failure. Even more patients could be helped with a kidney transplant if the rate of kidneys that are discarded and not transplanted could be reduced. Machine learning (ML) techniques can support decision-making in this context by early identification of donor organs at high risk of discard. Although various ML models have been applied, their results are difficult to compare due to heterogenous datasets and differences in feature engineering and evaluation strategies. This study aims to provide a systematic and reproducible comparison of ML models for donor-level kidney discard prediction. We trained five ML models: Logistic Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), and Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) along with an ensemble model on data from 4,080 deceased donors in Germany. We implemented a benchmarking framework, including standardized feature engineering, supervised feature selection, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. Model performance was assessed for discrimination, calibration, and explainability. The ensemble achieved the highest discrimination performance. However, the results did not differ significantly from those of LR. Individual models such as LR, RF, and MLP performed comparably and substantially better than DT. Platt scaling generally improved calibration. SHAP identified age and renal markers as dominant predictors across models, reflecting clinical plausibility. This study demonstrates that consistent data preprocessing, feature selection, and evaluation can be more decisive for predictive success than the choice of the ML algorithm. The proposed benchmarking framework enables transparent comparison of models and provides a reproducible foundation for improving donor-level kidney discard prediction.

entry.title: Robust Twoblock Simultaneous Dimension Reduction and Multivariate Regression

link.title: Robust Twoblock Simultaneous Dimension Reduction and Multivariate Regression

entry.content: This paper introduces robust twoblock (RTB) simultaneous dimension reduction, which is the first statistically robust method to perform simultaneous dimension reduction in two blocks of variables that allows to tune the number of components in each block individually. The paper proposes both a dense and a sparse version of the new method. Sparse RTB is the first robust estimator of this kind that allows to tune both the number of components and the degree of sparsity (i.e.\ the number of variables retained) for each block individually. RTB thereby allows to optimally extract and summarize the relevant portion of information in each block of data, also in the presence of outliers. As a corollary, the estimators can be recombined into a single estimate of regression coefficients for multivariate regression that is operable when the number of variables exceeds the number of cases in each block. An extensive simulation study illustrates that the new methods are resistant to different types of outliers, while maintaining estimation efficiency across a range of dimensionality settings. These findings both hold true for the dense and the sparse method. The methods’ performance is further illustrated on two example data sets and a straightforward algorithm is presented and made accessible in an open source repository.

entry.title: When the Prior Is Wrong: Probing Misspecified Diffusion Priors in Inverse Problems

link.title: When the Prior Is Wrong: Probing Misspecified Diffusion Priors in Inverse Problems

entry.content: While diffusion priors generate high-quality posterior samples across many scientific inverse problems, they are often trained on purely simulated data, thus inheriting the errors and biases of these underlying sources. Many approaches to adapting diffusion priors from a single observation require sufficient conflict between the data and the prior to successfully adapt and do not allow specific misspecification hypotheses to be tested. On the other hand, existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods determine whether the observation is compatible with a fixed prior, rather than specifying which assumptions to relax or by how much. To address these issues, we propose PIVOT: Prior Inference Via Observation-driven Transformations, which formulates diffusion prior misspecification as inference over an underlying latent variable representing a scientifically plausible discrepancy. By expanding the prior along these plausible directions of misspecification, PIVOT infers a posterior over the strength of each proposed discrepancy given the observation. This process can be efficiently amortized with just one posterior sampling pass using a conditional diffusion model. We also demonstrate how to determine if a proposed discrepancy is inconclusive because the measurement is too noisy or ill-posed. We validate PIVOT on seismic imaging and real-world black hole imaging problems, where we find that OOD observations generally lead to larger perturbation strengths when the proposed discrepancy family captures relevant components of the mismatch, as long as the discrepancy is visible to the measurement. PIVOT thereby provides an interpretable probe into how real-world priors could be misspecified.

entry.title: Variance-Aware Estimation and Inference for Michaelis–Menten Models with Heteroscedastic Errors and Clustered Measurements

link.title: Variance-Aware Estimation and Inference for Michaelis–Menten Models with Heteroscedastic Errors and Clustered Measurements

entry.content: Michaelis–Menten regression remains central to enzyme-kinetic analysis, yet routine applications still often rely on homoscedastic nonlinear least squares even when assay variability increases with substrate concentration or repeated readings are clustered. We develop original-scale Michaelis–Menten estimation and inference using semiparametric score equations for independent curves and a working-covariance extension for clustered assays. In simulation, heteroscedastic modeling improved variance recovery and shortened intervals in some scenarios relative to homoscedastic nonlinear least squares, while cluster-aware profile and NLME fits improved confidence-interval coverage for the maximum reaction velocity relative to pooled analyses that ignored clustering, with interval calibration depending on the number of independent clusters . We apply the proposed method to self-driving laboratory and soil exoenzyme data. The companion R package \texttt{inferMM , available on CRAN, implements the resulting workflow for single-curve, grouped, and clustered Michaelis–Menten analysis. \texttt{inferMM supports user-defined, fixed positive variance functions for single-curve and grouped estimation and inference. For independent single curves, it also accommodates non-Gaussian errors. These results show that simple variance-function and covariance modeling can stabilize enzyme-kinetic inference when variability changes with substrate concentration or measurements are clustered.

entry.title: Bias Correction for Scalar-on-Density Regression Models

link.title: Bias Correction for Scalar-on-Density Regression Models

entry.content: In one extension of scalar-on-function regression modeling, the covariate is taken to be a density that is estimated from a finite number of measurements gathered for each observational unit. When this number of measurements is relatively small, the estimated coefficient function suffers from attenuation bias. This paper studies how the bias depends on the number of measurements per unit and proposes a bias-correction method based on simulation extrapolation (SIMEX). We establish that the bias decreases monotonically as the number of measurements per unit increases. The proposed SIMEX procedure applies bootstrap resampling to simulate smaller measurement counts and then extrapolates to infinitely many measurements, thereby correcting finite-measurement bias. A comprehensive simulation study, conducted over a range of sample sizes and noise levels, shows that the mean integrated squared error of the coefficient function decreases with more measurements per unit and that the SIMEX-extrapolated estimates achieve lower bias than the naive estimates based on the full set of measurements. The practical utility of the method is further illustrated through an application to the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, for which we relate 24-hour physical activity profiles to all-cause mortality. This example supports the validity of the method and demonstrates its ability to detect and correct for finite-measurement bias.

entry.title: Critique of “Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses …” by John O’Quigley

link.title: Critique of “Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses …” by John O’Quigley

entry.content: The paper “Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses suspected of inflicting deliberate harm on patients” by Prof. John O’Quigley explores an interesting hypothesis concerning statistical information hidden in the part of the infamous Lucy Letby roster chart pertaining to the 37 other nurses. Unfortunately, we have to point out some serious errors in his statistical analyses. The data actually contains information which strongly disproves his main modelling assumption. We do, however, strongly agree with him that from a forensic statistical point of view, the roster chart is fake evidence which should not have been shown to jurors.

entry.title: Estimating Distributions with Failure Rate Properties from Noisy Quantile Data

link.title: Estimating Distributions with Failure Rate Properties from Noisy Quantile Data

entry.content: Estimating an unknown cumulative distribution function (cdf) is fundamental both as a statistical goal and as an input to downstream optimization. In practice, however, distribution estimation is often complicated by incomplete knowledge of the distribution’s structure and limited, censored data. We address the first challenge by studying distributions with failure-rate shape constraints, especially increasing failure rate (IFR), without assuming a fully specified parametric family. To address the second, we consider noisy quantile data: at finitely many prespecified knots, each observation records only whether an independent sample lies below or above the knot. This setting arises naturally in pricing, reliability, and healthcare. We formulate the IFR-constrained maximum likelihood estimator and show that the original problem is infinite-dimensional and non-convex. Our two-step approach solves a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem over transformed knot values, then reconstructs a full cdf through shape-preserving interpolation. We establish finite-sample error bounds and convergence rates that guide offline data collection. We also show how the framework accommodates additional properties: (i) decreasing failure rate, (ii) failure rate average, (iii) generalized failure rate, and (iv) new better than used. Numerical experiments and case studies in revenue management and reliability illustrate improved goodness of fit and downstream decision quality.

entry.title: The Continuous Latent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Dynamics Framework: A Lyapunov-based Multivariate Latent Process Model for Longitudinal Categorical Data

link.title: The Continuous Latent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Dynamics Framework: A Lyapunov-based Multivariate Latent Process Model for Longitudinal Categorical Data

entry.content: Longitudinal biomedical studies increasingly collect irregularly sampled, multivariate categorical measurements that are noisy manifestations of underlying continuous disease processes. These data pose several challenges: subjects exhibit heterogeneous progression patterns; multiple observed items reflect unobserved biological traits that may evolve interdependently; and observation schedules often have unequal intervals both within and across subjects. To address these challenges, we present the Continuous Latent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Dynamics (CLOUD) framework for modeling complex disease trajectories from multivariate longitudinal categorical data. CLOUD links multivariate categorical observations to underlying latent functional domains and characterizes their coupled temporal evolution by integrating item response theory, factor analysis, and multivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes. Methodologically, we introduce a time-inhomogeneous OU process that incorporates covariate-dependent progression slopes into the moving mean function of the latent dynamics, allowing baseline biomarkers and clinical characteristics to modulate individual disease trajectories while preserving the analytical tractability of the OU process. We further propose a Lyapunov-based structural parameterization of the joint drift and stationary covariance that enforces valid dynamics by construction and enables efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. We establish well-posedness and conditional identifiability. Under additional regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic properties of the model. Through simulation studies and an application to Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative data, we demonstrate that CLOUD can characterize subject-specific disease evolution across multiple interacting functional domains.

entry.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

link.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

entry.content: Semicontinuous outcomes characterized by an exact zero mass and heavy-tailed continuous distributions challenge empirical risk modeling and machine learning. Compound Poisson-Gamma Tweedie processes impose a rigid mean-variance coupling that distorts zero-mass probabilities under extreme tail dispersion, flattening continuous density and reducing extreme-risk discrimination. Furthermore, heuristic post-hoc target capping introduces systematic bias while leaving loss gradients vulnerable to tail leverage. We present a unified, statistically coherent likelihood framework for semicontinuous modeling under arbitrary zero-inflation and explicit upper boundary constraints. Optimization and likelihood evaluations operate strictly in a latent space defined by the power-scaling mapping $y_i^* = \min{(y_i/s)^\lambda, U^*}$, where $s \in (0, U)$ anchors scale and $\lambda \in (0,1)$ regularizes tail curvature. The architecture partitions the response into three regimes: an unconstrained Bernoulli hurdle, an analytical continuous Gamma body, and an upper boundary point mass governed by incomplete Gamma survival ratios. Rather than an arbitrary truncation, the boundary functions as an intrinsic tail accumulator bounding score and Hessian dynamics. We derive the closed-form deviance objective, score vectors, and block-diagonal Hessian matrix, proving that parameter spaces are information-orthogonal to enable concurrent classification and regression updates. Asymptotic boundary analysis demonstrates that score and curvature scale linearly in the deep tail, establishing a quadratic restoring force that prevents gradient collapse. The framework breaks the Tweedie parameter rigidity paradox while maintaining structural fidelity across both zero occurrence and extreme severity differentiation.

entry.title: Distribution-Free Changepoint Inference for Rainfall Patterns

link.title: Distribution-Free Changepoint Inference for Rainfall Patterns

entry.content: Long records of rainfall contain critical information about the temporal organization of precipitation within a year, including wet and dry spells. Detecting when this temporal pattern changes is central to climate-impact assessment and environmental monitoring.A common data structure features observations from m locations over T years. For location i and year t, the record is a vector of daily measurements $X_{i,t} = (X_{i,t,1}, …, X_{i,t,D})^\top$, with D = 365. The goal is to identify an unknown year $t_0$ when the temporal rainfall pattern changes across the region. Because changes in the intra-annual pattern affect the frequency-domain behavior of the daily sequence, we represent each yearly curve through a spectral feature capturing the strength of temporal oscillation at a fixed frequency.Classical changepoint methods often rely on parametric likelihoods or Gaussian approximations, which are hard to justify for skewed and heavy-tailed rainfall data. Furthermore, many procedures only return a point estimate. A confidence set for the change year is crucial in environmental applications to quantify temporal uncertainty and distinguish sharp transitions from weak evidence.This paper develops a distribution-free framework for detecting a synchronized structural change in yearly rainfall patterns across independently monitored locations. For each location-year pair, we compute a fixed-frequency nonparametric spectral density estimate. These features form a $T \times m$ data matrix. By exploiting the exchangeability of yearly spectral features before and after the true changepoint, alongside spatial independence, we construct finite-sample valid confidence sets for the unknown change year.

entry.title: Evaluating laser scanning data sources, canopy metrics, and predictor resolution for forest inventory

link.title: Evaluating laser scanning data sources, canopy metrics, and predictor resolution for forest inventory

entry.content: Forest managers updating growing stock volume (GSV) estimates must decide whether existing LiDAR data calibrated with current inventory are sufficient or a new acquisition provides worthwhile improvements. We compared regional airborne laser scanning (ALS) acquired in 2023 with uncrewed aerial vehicle laser scanning (ULS) from 2026 in a mixed-species forest in north-eastern Germany. Both datasets were calibrated using the same 2026 personal laser scanning inventory within a change-of-support regression framework. We compared 3 m and 35 m grids, canopy height alone and with three structural metrics, and models with and without spatial random effects. Evaluation comprised 10-fold cross-validation (CV) on 118 undisturbed plots (no tree removal), prediction on 33 disturbed plots (detected removal) excluded from calibration, and CV across all 151 plots. In undisturbed CV, the lowest root mean squared prediction errors (RMSPEs) were 74.1 m3 ha-1 for ULS and 81.5 m3 ha-1 for ALS, a 9.1% reduction for ULS. Both used spatial effects and 3 m predictors, with structural metrics for ULS and canopy height only for ALS. At 3 m, canopy-height-only models performed similarly across sources, whereas adding structural metrics improved ULS predictions. Finer grids improved both sources, and spatial effects gave only small gains. On the disturbed holdout, 3 m ULS models had little bias, whereas ALS overpredicted volume, consistent with predictors representing pre-removal conditions. Canopy-height-only ULS outperformed the four-predictor models on these plots. Across all 151 plots, the 3 m four-predictor ULS models achieved an RMSPE of 70.5 m3 ha-1 versus 81.5 m3 ha-1 for the best ALS model, a 13.5% reduction. Existing ALS therefore retained substantial predictive value on undisturbed plots, while ULS provided additional information and supported estimation across both disturbance classes.

entry.title: Extreme Binary Classification: Extreme Value Theory for Extreme Constraint on False Negative

link.title: Extreme Binary Classification: Extreme Value Theory for Extreme Constraint on False Negative

entry.content: While binary classification is one of the most extensively studied problems in machine learning, the regime in which the goal is to learn a classifier with an almost zero false negative rate remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce the Extreme Binary Classification problem, where the objective is to learn a classifier whose false negative rate $\alpha$ is constrained by $\epsilon_{N_1}=o_{N_1\to\infty}(1/N_1)$, with $N_1$ denoting the number of positive examples in the training set. To address this problem, we propose a threshold adaptation method theoretically grounded in guarantees derived from Extreme Value Theory, together with a feature selection procedure based on a permutation test applied to sample maxima. Experimental results on four real-world datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that our approach compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods. In addition, we illustrate its interpretability through an application to a cancer screening dataset.

entry.title: The LR2 Lifetime Distribution: Rate Crossing, Reliability Properties, and Estimation

link.title: The LR2 Lifetime Distribution: Rate Crossing, Reliability Properties, and Estimation

entry.content: We study the LR2 one-parameter lifetime distribution obtained by mixing an exponential component of rate $\theta/2$ and a gamma component with shape four and rate $\theta^2$. The exponential mixing probability is $\theta^2/(1+\theta^2)$ for $\theta>0$. We derive the density, survival function, moments, transforms, truncated moments, quantiles, order-statistic distributions, mean residual life, and stress–strength reliability. Identifiability follows from the density at the origin, and strict monotonicity of the mean yields a unique moment estimator. A complete density-turning-point criterion and analytic initial and tail hazard expansions clarify the possible shapes. The component rates cross at one half. The hazard decreases initially for every positive parameter and eventually increases in the gamma-dominated regime; it eventually decreases in the exponential-dominated regime. We develop likelihood estimation, observed information, constrained expectation–maximization, spacing estimation, and inference under regularity conditions, and state the likelihood for independent right censoring. A reproducible Monte Carlo study with eight settings and 4,000 generated samples compares likelihood and moment estimation and evaluates log-scale confidence intervals. The analysis distinguishes mathematical properties from empirical validation and explains the restrictions associated with a fixed working time unit.

entry.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks

link.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks

entry.content: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.96 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

entry.title: Functional nestedness of soil nematode communities across Europe: integrating morphological counts and eDNA reads

link.title: Functional nestedness of soil nematode communities across Europe: integrating morphological counts and eDNA reads

entry.content: 1. Soil nematodes occupy multiple trophic positions and contribute to key processes in soil food webs. Their communities vary across land uses and environmental conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these differences mainly reflect taxon replacement or nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 2. Here, we analysed two independent European datasets of soil nematode communities, SOB4ES, based on eDNA metabarcoding, and NemEu, based on morphological identification, to examine how genus composition varies across land uses. We partitioned community dissimilarity into turnover and nestedness-resultant components and compared sites under contrasting land uses with those sharing the same land use, while accounting for geographical and soil-related variation. We also assessed matrix-level nestedness, differences among trophic groups and associations between genus composition and environmental gradients. 3. In both datasets, genus turnover was consistently greater between contrasting land uses than within the same land use. Although the differences were modest, they remained significant after accounting for geographical distance and genus richness, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity contributed little to land-use differentiation. These findings suggest that land-use-associated differences in European nematode communities are expressed primarily through changes in genus identity rather than nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 4. The consistency of this result across independently assembled datasets supports the broader relevance of taxonomic turnover for understanding soil biodiversity patterns across European land uses.

entry.title: Bayesian Computation of Copula-based Multivariate Models with an Application to Doping Detection

link.title: Bayesian Computation of Copula-based Multivariate Models with an Application to Doping Detection

entry.content: The Athlete Biological Passport (ABP) monitors athletes for doping by comparing their biomarker readings against personalized reference ranges. These are estimated via the Bayesian ADAPTIVE model, which analyzes biomarkers separately and ignores their dependence. Building on a recently proposed copula-based multivariate extension of ADAPTIVE, this paper focuses on its computational aspects, introducing a fully joint MCMC algorithm and comparing it with a two-step Bayesian IFM estimator. Simulations show the two procedures perform comparably under a correctly specified copula, but exhibit a genuine trade-off under misspecification: the Bayesian IFM protects marginal inference, while the joint MCMC yields better-calibrated dependence estimates and is markedly faster. The two approaches are tested on a dataset containing ABP profiles of elite athletes, provided by NADO Italia, and collected as part of the project “Enhancing the methodological framework for doping detection: from univariate to multivariate testing analysis on Athlete Biological Passport profiles”. Both approaches achieve consistent classification performance, providing anti-doping organizations with two concrete inferential routes for adopting a multivariate ADAPTIVE model, along with guidance on the trade-offs between them.

entry.title: A Tensor Neural Network for Interpretable and Predictive Representations

link.title: A Tensor Neural Network for Interpretable and Predictive Representations

entry.content: Tensor regression is challenged by the exponential dimensionality of tensor-valued covariates and their complex multi-mode dependence. Existing methods therefore often rely on simple models, such as linear tensor regression and tensor additive models, which are computationally tractable but impose restrictive structural assumptions and may limit predictive accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose a tensor neural network that learns low-dimensional, interpretable, and prediction-sufficient representations while preserving the multi-mode structure of tensor data. The model captures nonlinear effects for accurate response prediction while retaining the interpretability of classical linear tensor regression. Theoretically, we establish selection consistency for the minimal representation dimension $K^$ necessary for prediction and show that the estimator attains a representation-adaptive non-asymptotic error rate. Specifically, the rate improves from the ambient-dimensional order $n^{-\frac{\beta}{\mathcal{D}+2\beta}}$ to $n^{-\frac{\beta}{K^+2\beta}}$, where $\mathcal{D}=\prod_{j=1}^M P_j$ is the ambient dimension. This demonstrates that recovering the low-dimensional representation is crucial for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in tensor regression. Moreover, minimizing the derived generalization error bound yields explicit tuning-parameter choices for computationally lightweight tuning. Extensive simulations and real-data analyses show consistent performance across settings of varying complexity. Unlike black-box deep learning models, the framework supports direct visualization and interpretation of learned tensor representations without external post hoc tools.

entry.title: Code availability is not enough: schemas for documenting and extending data analysis

link.title: Code availability is not enough: schemas for documenting and extending data analysis

entry.content: A data analysis involves a sequence of decisions, from data cleaning to model specification, each of which can affect the reported result. Reproducing that result is not the same as understanding the sequence of decisions that produced it and the reasons for each: the code mixes those decisions with implementation details, while the manuscript states the major decisions and their rationale but scatters them across its sections and often leaves out the minor ones. A reader may then ask how the result would change under a different decision: the question itself is easy to pose, but implementing it is often non-trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a schema that represents a data analysis as a collection of decisions in natural language, from which large language models (LLMs) can generate and validate analysis scripts directly. This workflow can also expand a single analysis into a full multiverse of alternatives, specified in an alternative file, ready for comparison. We demonstrate the proposed workflow in two applications. In the first, we construct a schema for a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data and show that it reproduces the reported estimates, and that a reviewer-suggested alternative can be specified through the alternative file and turned into code automatically. In the second, where no schema is provided, we show how the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility check, applied to the many-analysts football study. As an intermediate representation between the manuscript and code scripts, our schema gives a self-contained account of an analysis and makes it extensible from a reader’s perspective.

entry.title: B-SLIM: BART Sparse Linear Interactions Model for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

link.title: B-SLIM: BART Sparse Linear Interactions Model for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

entry.content: Estimating covariate-dependent treatment effects is a central challenge in personalized medicine. Existing approaches often emphasize either fully parametric models, risking misspecification, or flexible machine learning methods, which may require large samples to detect the small treatment effect heterogeneity common in medical settings. We propose B-SLIM (BART Sparse Linear Interaction Model), a semi-parametric model for causal inference that combines a flexible Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) prognostic component with a sparse linear treatment effect component. This hybrid structure combines flexible prognosis modelling with interpretable treatment effects. The treatment effect component includes main effects and pairwise interactions, regularized through a global-local shrinkage prior. entry.title: When precision exceeds fidelity: systematic error quantification for inference with misspecified simulators

link.title: When precision exceeds fidelity: systematic error quantification for inference with misspecified simulators

entry.content: As scientific datasets grow in complexity and precision, the primary source of uncertainty in parameter inference shifts from measurement noise to systematic errors within the simulators themselves. In this setting, Bayesian evidence concentrates on whichever misspecified model best approximates the data. Evidence-weighted model averaging can then underestimate systematic uncertainty when one model component compensates for the misspecification of another component. We posit that in this case, the key question is how each model responds to discrepancies between simulator and data. We show that the local response of an inferred parameter to perturbations in the data — the model’s influence map — can be estimated efficiently from forward evaluations of the simulator at existing posterior samples. Propagating discrepancy residuals through these influence maps enables individual sources of systematic bias to be isolated. Applied to independent observations used to infer the mass of a supermassive black hole, we find that the error is dominated by model systematics. We identify a simplification shared by all models, propagate the discrepancies through each model’s influence map, and apply a first-order correction of the resulting biases. This substantially improves the cross-observation consistency of the inferred black-hole mass within each model while preserving the between-model spread that represents remaining systematics.

entry.title: A Quantile-Based Framework for Bimodal Distribution Construction

link.title: A Quantile-Based Framework for Bimodal Distribution Construction

entry.content: This study suggests a novel quantile-based framework to construct bimodal distribution which does not rely on mixture representations or closed-form probability density functions. This proposed approach induces bimodality by transforming the quantile density through a strictly positive modulation function so that it can preserve the support and tail behavior of a chosen baseline distribution with providing explicit control over modal structure. The method is shown to apply broadly across bounded, semi-bounded and unbounded distribution families which include power, reflected power, logistic, Weibull and generalized lambda distributions. Simulation studies and a real-data application were performed which have shown that the proposed construction yields smooth, interpretable and computationally stable bimodal models and it also provides a flexible alternative to classical mixture-based approaches. Also this framework allows gradual transitions between unimodal and bimodal shapes which make it well suited for modeling overlapping regimes which are commonly encountered in real-world data. This proposed methodology therefor offers a robust and interpretable tool for bimodal modeling without requiring latent class assumptions or complex estimation procedures.

entry.title: Horseshoe-Type Shrinkage from Ratio-Generated Priors

link.title: Horseshoe-Type Shrinkage from Ratio-Generated Priors

entry.content: We develop a class of horseshoe-type shrinkage priors generated by ratios of independent numerator and denominator random variables. Large denominator values produce concentration near zero, small denominator values generate heavy tails, and the numerator determines scale and geometry and may also influence tail behavior. We establish general origin and tail asymptotics, including power and logarithmic singularities. Under a Gaussian likelihood and regularly varying prior tails, the posterior mean approaches the observation for large signals, with risk approaching that of the unshrunk observation. The denominator also induces a latent shrinkage factor. For a Cauchy denominator, this factor has exactly the ${\rm Beta}(1/2,1/2)$ distribution, whatever the numerator. With a Gaussian numerator and appropriate scale calibration, it recovers the classical horseshoe shrinkage coefficient, whereas non-Gaussian numerators can change the effective posterior shrinkage, even in its asymptotic rate. The Cauchy/Cauchy prior illustrates the theory, with a logarithmic singularity at the origin in one dimension, power singularities in higher dimensions, and logarithmically modified Cauchy-order tails. Its posterior mean shrinks smoothly, whereas its spatial median behaves nearly as a threshold rule. We also compare the Cauchy/Cauchy posterior mean with fifteen established shrinkage procedures on the four standard Donoho-Johnstone test functions, finding competitive, though not uniformly superior, wavelet-denoising performance. The ratio construction generalizes several published shrinkage priors and offers a flexible framework for sparse estimation, with natural applications to wavelet shrinkage, variable selection, and structured multivariate shrinkage.

entry.title: Addressing Missing Exposures in Causal Inference: A Practical Guide

link.title: Addressing Missing Exposures in Causal Inference: A Practical Guide

entry.content: Missing exposure data are a common challenge in epidemiologic studies that can complicate the identification and estimation of causal effects. Particularly for researchers constructing doubly-robust estimators, it can be unclear how to adapt standard methods such as augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) to account for missing exposures. This paper clarifies challenges posed by missing exposures, and discusses approaches available for doubly-robust estimation in these settings. We outline numerous mechanisms that can give rise to missing exposures in practice, and demonstrate why double-robustness alone does not protect complete-case AIPW from missing exposure bias. We highlight three broad approaches for addressing this bias: multiply-robust estimation, single imputation and multiple imputation. Using complete-data AIPW—the estimator one would construct in the absence of missing data—as a benchmark, we demonstrate how these approaches impute different components of the ideal complete-data estimator. We discuss practical implementation challenges, including whether outcome information should be used to impute exposures or predict exposure missingness. Through simulations, we illustrate the critical roles of the missingness mechanism, treatment effect heterogeneity and model specification on the performance of these approaches. We conclude with recommendations to help researchers choose an analysis strategy and inform modeling choices involved in their implementation.

entry.title: Geodesic Causal Forests: Learning Heterogeneous Treatment Effects for Random Objects

link.title: Geodesic Causal Forests: Learning Heterogeneous Treatment Effects for Random Objects

entry.content: Causal forests and orthogonal learners estimate heterogeneous treatment effects for scalar or Euclidean outcomes, yet outcomes are increasingly random objects, such as compositions, covariance matrices, distributions, or networks, in metric spaces without linear structure. We introduce geodesic causal forests for conditional geodesic treatment effects. Geodesic transport moves each geodesic between conditional Fr'echet means of the potential outcomes to a common reference, making effects comparable across individuals. Because random objects cannot be added or subtracted, Euclidean residual corrections are unavailable; we instead correct the squared-distance loss through which the forest selects splits and estimates effects. The loss is real-valued for every candidate effect, so the correction requires only Fr'echet means and leaves second-order nuisance error; for Euclidean outcomes, it recovers doubly robust learning. We establish consistency, convergence rates, and split-selection guarantees under conditions verified for curved and nonsmooth spaces. In simulations with covariance-matrix outcomes, the correction substantially reduces estimation error. For women’s livelihood compositions in BRAC’s randomized antipoverty program in Bangladesh, new livestock work mainly replaces casual wage work; after alignment, a single effect reproduces much of the variation in percentage-point changes across baseline activities, and the fitted effects are largest among former domestic workers and older women.

link.title: Adaptive confidence bands for a continuous treatment effect curve under shape constraints

entry.content: In causal inference with observational data new inferential targets arise when treatment is continuous rather than discrete. Here we form (simultaneous) confidence bands over the continuous treatment effect curve. We form confidence bands based on assuming the curve satisfies shape constraints of either monotonicity or concavity, under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. As is commonly the case, two nuisance functions arise, and our bands are asymptotically valid if the product of the error rates of the two nuisance functions is small enough. We also develop non-causal shape constrained bands in regression with fixed or random non-uniform grid which are of independent interest. Furthermore, our bands are adaptive to a range of function flatness and smoothness levels in that when the true flatness/smoothness level is unknown the bands still achieve the same (optimal) rate of convergence (in sup-norm) as when the true smoothness level is known. We demonstrate these bands through simulations and an application to the effect of nurse staffing on hospital performance.

entry.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration

link.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration

entry.content: Ensemble-based methods provide a practical framework for history matching, prediction, and optimization of subsurface models. In methodological studies, however, performance is rarely assessed from a single run. Comparisons typically span cases, configurations, and random seeds, while each evaluation may require an expensive external simulator. Keeping such studies computationally bounded, auditable, and reproducible therefore requires more than implementing a numerical method: experiments must be validated before execution, computational costs estimated, repeated runs organized consistently, and configurations and outputs made traceable. To address these needs, we developed APEX (Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration), an open-source Python platform that provides a common framework for configuring, validating, executing, recording, and comparing ensemble-based experiments. APEX is organized around three concepts: an experiment defines what is executed, a run records a single execution, and a study coordinates and compares multiple experiments or runs. Experiments are specified through validated configurations, which can also be generated by a planner agent. Before execution, APEX estimates the maximum number of forward simulations required. If the estimate exceeds a user-defined threshold, submission is held for approval. Each run records provenance information, while studies repeat problems across variants and paired replicates and compare results using paired statistical analyses. Scientific and computational components, including methods, simulators, metrics, and optimizers, are implemented as plugins. A command line interface, Python client, REST service with a web interface, and tools for language model agents access these capabilities through a common service layer.

entry.title: Functional Direct Binomial Regression for Right-Censored Competing Risks Data

link.title: Functional Direct Binomial Regression for Right-Censored Competing Risks Data

entry.content: Existing regression-based methods for functional predictors often overlook right-censored competing risks outcomes, limiting their applicability in many biomedical studies. To address this gap, this article proposes a functional direct binomial model for right-censored competing risks data, where a binary outcome indicates the occurrence of an event of interest before a fixed time horizon. The model enables straightforward prediction of the cumulative incidence function, can be fitted using standard, scalable algorithms for large-scale studies, and has broad applications to functional predictors, such as wearable device data. We establish large-sample theory to facilitate inference, including hypothesis testing and the construction of confidence intervals and bands for both scalar coefficients and functional parameters. The methodology is further extended to accommodate multiple functional biomarkers and to handle missing failure causes. Simulation studies confirm that the proposed method provides accurate estimation and valid inference. We illustrate the approach with an application to modeling time to advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the presence of the competing risk of death, leveraging continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data and baseline covariates. The analysis shows that CGM is both a significant predictor and a viable alternative to the traditional HbA1c biomarker for CKD.

entry.title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework

link.title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework

entry.content: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to integrate both types through a common two-parameter logistic item response model and fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood estimation. The framework includes binary-only models in common-scale evaluation without discarding available probabilityinformation; broader measurement coverage does not by itself ensure greater precision or measurement equivalence. Simulations evaluate statistical efficiency when both response types have the same expected value. Moreover, adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents. However, adding noisier binary responses to an already precise probability sample can increase estimation error under equal observation weights. An application to Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) combines probability response data from the Open LLM Leaderboard with binary response data from Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and reveals model-family response patterns, differences in item characteristics, and systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols. The proposed framework extends common-scale IRT evaluation to models with different response formats while highlighting the roles of observation variability and evaluation-protocol comparability in statistical efficiency and interpretation.

link.title: An iterative procedure for statistical calibration

entry.content: We study the iterative proportional fitting procedure (IPFP) under multiple pushforward constraints, motivated by model calibration. The goal is to find a distribution on model parameters whose pushforward by models matches data distributions. The classic convergence result of IPFP under marginal constraints establish convergence of IPFP under suitable regularity conditions and develop a variant of sequential importance sampling to approximate the iterative procedure. We also propose a related procedure for constructing a high probability parameter region. Simulation studies illustrate the performance of these methods. Finally, we apply IPFP to COVID19 ensemble forecasting. Variation of Covid strains across regions can lead to variation in surge rates and thus affect forecasting accuracy. To capture the variation, we estimate a probability distribution of epidemiological model parameters using early stage surge data from an ensemble of regions. We then propagate the distribution through the model to forecast both the ensemble’s overall trend and its variability.

entry.content: The paper introduces a Change point Hypothesis Assessment for Significance in Multivariate data (CHASM) - a novel non-parametric approach for evaluating the significance of change points detected in multivariate data, especially relevant for a trustworthy autonomous industrial system. The method is highly scalable, doesn’t require data labeling, and allows for customizable evaluation criteria, such as inter-component relationships. Its non-parametric nature broadens applicability to non-Gaussian distributed data. CHASM incorporates robust auxiliary statistics that maintain reliability even in the presence of outliers, enabling accurate assessment of change point significance for complex data. Beyond statistical significance testing, CHASM also facilitates root-cause analysis of detected changes. It offers a solution expected by practitioners for validating change points identified by segmentation-based algorithms, particularly those lacking rigorous statistical foundations. To support situation aware decision making, a {trustworthy factor} is introduced and its performance demonstrated for simulated and real-world data recorded in machine monitoring system. Using MAPE, it was evidenced that the two-stage procedure - identification of the change point and authorization of the change point - significantly outperforms (23-fold in the reported experiment) the one-stage scheme. All these are essential in real-world applications, where overfitting and false alarms can lead to loss of trust in technical solutions.

entry.title: Sharp sensitivity bounds and maximin policy learning under violations of principal ignorability

link.title: Sharp sensitivity bounds and maximin policy learning under violations of principal ignorability

entry.content: Identification of assignment effects among compliers often relies on the untestable assumption of principal ignorability. Sensitivity analyses based only on outcome means and ranges can admit complier distributions incompatible with the observed data. We develop a distributional sensitivity model preserving the full observed outcome distributions and identified complier proportions. The challenge is to recover latent complier distributions within observed mixtures while ensuring compatibility across assignment arms. We characterize exactly which pairs arise from a single compatible full-data law, obtaining sharp bounds on effects and policy values. This characterization shows how complier proportions constrain departures from principal ignorability and why informative bounds remain without a finite sensitivity restriction. Accounting for principal scores in both population weights and sensitivity limits, we establish conditions for doubly robust consistency, semiparametric efficiency, and conservative bounds under quantile misspecification. Double robustness requires consistent principal score estimation. We also develop maximin decision-tree policies with value consistency and inference guarantees. Numerical studies demonstrate gains from retaining distributional information, and an Oregon Health Insurance Experiment application examines implications for complier effects and assignment policies.

entry.title: Refinements to precision-information imputation in meta-analysis of survival rates: Boundary correction and cross-study borrowing

link.title: Refinements to precision-information imputation in meta-analysis of survival rates: Boundary correction and cross-study borrowing

entry.content: Meta-analyses of survival rates require precision information, such as standard errors (SEs), which is often unreported. We previously proposed imputing missing SEs from reported survival rates, sample sizes, and risk-set sizes. The original method has two limitations. First, it replaces Kaplan–Meier estimates of 1 with 0.99 regardless of sample size. Second, when the risk-set size is unavailable, it uses the total event count as a fallback. The count is often unreported, and the fallback can also substantially overestimate SEs. We propose a sample-size-dependent boundary correction based on a pseudo-event and a method that borrows time-specific event information from studies with available risk-set sizes. In simulations, the boundary correction was more stable than fixed replacement, and borrowing reduced study-level SE imputation bias. Borrowing generally improved precision by retaining studies with missing SEs that lacked both risk-set sizes and event counts.

entry.title: A Robust Approach for Regression Analysis of Panel Count Data with Time-varying Covariates

link.title: A Robust Approach for Regression Analysis of Panel Count Data with Time-varying Covariates

entry.content: The validity of statistical inference for panel count data with time-varying covariates depends on the correct specification of within-subject correlation structures; misspecification often leads to questionable inference. To alleviate, robust inference has been proposed for mean models, which implicitly assume monotone mean functions. When covariate values fluctuate with time, however, the assumed monotonicity becomes unrealistic. In this research, we propose a robust inference based on rate models that are free of such constraints. Since the asymptotic variance has no closed form under the rate model, we further develop computationally efficient robust variance estimators using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, thus sidestepping the need for computationally intensive numerical methods, which could undermine the robustness. Rigorous theoretical development is provided in support of parameter estimation and inference. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method. We present a real clinical application to illustrate the use of the proposed method.

entry.title: New fast and accurate estimators of the five-parameter lambda distribution (FPLD) with practical applications

link.title: New fast and accurate estimators of the five-parameter lambda distribution (FPLD) with practical applications

entry.content: When fitting parametric densities, simple distributions are often chosen because they are computationally efficient to estimate and easy to interpret. However, simplicity can result in important features of the data being missed. This paper introduces fast and reliable estimators of the five-parameter lambda distribution (FPLD). The FPLD is highly flexible, can take many different shapes, and provides greater control over skewness and tail behaviour than distributions with fewer parameters. Simulations are provided to demonstrate the excellent performance of the proposed estimators compared with existing methods, at a fraction of the computational cost. Applications in which speed and accuracy are important are also provided, with comparisons to commonly used but potentially overly simplistic approaches. Finally, an R package implementing the proposed estimators and a web application that allows users to determine the FPLD parameters required to approximate well-known distributions are provided.

entry.title: How Many Sources, Not Just How Many Problems: Planning the Precision of LLM Evaluations from Earlier Results

link.title: How Many Sources, Not Just How Many Problems: Planning the Precision of LLM Evaluations from Earlier Results

entry.content: When benchmark problems share sources, such as variants of one template or tasks from one repository, an evaluation budget must fix the number of sources as well as the number of problems. We ask whether pilot data or earlier evaluation results can predict, before an evaluation is run, how much the standard deviation (SD) of the score grows when the same budget is concentrated on fewer sources. We use the classical design effect with an intraclass correlation estimated on data disjoint from those used to check the prediction. On GSM-Symbolic, 100 problems drawn as 10 templates x 10 variants have an SD of 9.2 pp against 2.7 pp from 100 templates; pilot data on 15 other questions predict the ratio as 3.49 against 3.52 measured on held-out questions (medians over 20 splits; single splits err by -13% to +16%), once the actual sampling plan is included. On SWE-bench Verified, 10 randomly selected public submissions predict the median ratio for 119 other submissions within 3% for 2 or more repositories, and 3 submissions are nearly as good. Dropping the finite-population terms from the design prediction gives errors of 13-21% on GSM-Symbolic, where it reduces to the textbook formula, and 25-35% on SWE-bench. Widening iid intervals by the square root of the pilot design effect brings pass@1 coverage on concentrated designs to 0.93-0.98, but not pass@16 (0.85, 0.76). We also report two lessons for anyone validating such predictions: split pilot and held-out data by question source, not by difficulty version, and do not read a good fit of the formula as evidence of source clustering (MATH-500). The method is not new; we contribute a held-out test of its advance predictions and a recipe for using them. Code: https://github.com/Guang627/deff-eval

entry.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data

link.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data

entry.content: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$–$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system’s response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.

entry.title: Cutting Bus Service Without Cutting Access: Persistent Homology of Service Deserts and Timetable Reductions

link.title: Cutting Bus Service Without Cutting Access: Persistent Homology of Service Deserts and Timetable Reductions

entry.content: Japanese bus operators are withdrawing service for lack of drivers, and the choice of which trips to withdraw determines who keeps a bus. We measure service at each stop from vehicle GPS and smart-card records, without timetables, and use persistent homology of walking and walking-plus-waiting time to find enclosed service deserts: pockets surrounded by service but beyond walking distance from it. Around Tsukuba, 35 such pockets lie more than 800m from any station or hourly stop. The 17 that are fully ringed by walkable service hold 18,446 residents. We compare two 2020 timetable reductions by Kanto Railway with random reductions and a heuristic frontier of same-size, capacity-feasible alternatives. At two and four buses an hour, both reductions protected service better than random reductions. No alternative found by the sweep dominates the state-of-emergency timetable. The summer timetable is dominated: it withdrew hourly service from 5,253 residents around stops with almost no morning riders, whereas same-size alternatives kept it for all of them at equal waiting. Averages hide a tail: under the actual timetables, 5.9% and 3.9% of residents are at stops whose expected wait rises by 10 minutes or more, against 0.5% and 0.3% in the alternatives, and capping the increase at 10 minutes at every served stop is feasible at the operator’s sizes. If half the removed hours become paid hours saved, the labor saving of both reductions and their main alternatives fall short of the fare revenue on the removed trips.

entry.title: Bayesian Latent Functional Mediation Analysis with Application to Population-Scale Single-Cell Data

link.title: Bayesian Latent Functional Mediation Analysis with Application to Population-Scale Single-Cell Data

entry.content: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing studies pair cell-level gene expression with donor-level genotypes, enabling investigation of genetic regulation across cellular states. Mediation analysis in this setting must account for cells nested within donors and for unobserved cellular states. We propose a Bayesian latent functional mediation model that decomposes the association between genotype and distal gene expression into a component mediated through a candidate cis gene and a remaining direct component. The model represents expression as donor-specific trajectories over a shared latent state coordinate constrained by coarse cell annotations. Joint inference propagates uncertainty in latent states, trajectories, and mediation parameters into state-specific effect functions and their integrated summaries. Simulations show that effect recovery improves with the number of donors and that averaging expression within donors can change the mediated and direct components even when the total association is preserved. In 403,087 CD4+ T cells from 961 OneK1K donors, higher rs1131017 G-allele dosage was associated with higher RPS26 expression across the fitted state domain. The estimated RPS26-mediated component of the association with BAX expression was negative over most of the domain and was partly offset by a positive direct component, yielding a smaller negative integrated total association. In sensitivity analyses conditional on estimated donor trajectories, all three integrated effects retained their signs, with 95% credible intervals excluding zero, at the five examined coefficient-level residual correlations with $ \rho_s \leq 0.3$. The mediated and direct effects reversed signs at $\rho_s=-0.5$, while the integrated total association remained negative across all seven tested settings.

entry.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty

link.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty

entry.content: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.

entry.title: Learning to Infer: Statistical Inference through Meta Learning

link.title: Learning to Infer: Statistical Inference through Meta Learning

entry.content: We study meta learning for statistical inference, in which neural networks learn inference rules from simulated tasks and apply them to new datasets without parameter updates, providing a form of in-context learning. We draw on statistical decision theory to design training objectives whose population minimizers are Bayes rules and exploit their connections to classical inference procedures to establish frequentist guarantees for the learned rules. The structure of classical inference procedures also motivates the design of our neural network architecture, called Residual Recurrent Deep Sets (RRDS), which repeatedly aggregates information across observations in a permutation-invariant manner and refines its internal state through residual updates. Under suitable regularity and training conditions, we establish asymptotic efficiency in parameter estimation, consistency in model selection, and variable selection guarantees in high-dimensional regression models. The RRDS architecture allows us to avoid the curse of sample size that arises in generic neural network approximation when the network takes the entire dataset as input. For fixed-dimensional models, the network size and the number of meta training tasks need only grow polynomially in the sample size; under additional analyticity conditions, these requirements improve to polylogarithmic growth in network size and nearly linear growth in the number of training tasks. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample advantages of the learned inference rules over classical methods.

entry.title: Don’t Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization

link.title: Don’t Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization

entry.content: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population’s potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.
