entry.title: Shooting for Fit: Risk-Averse Stochastic Roster Construction from Bayesian Shot-Pattern Models

link.title: Shooting for Fit: Risk-Averse Stochastic Roster Construction from Bayesian Shot-Pattern Models

entry.content: Roster construction is a critical decision problem in professional basketball, requiring teams to balance player quality, player complementarity, and financial constraints under uncertainty. Existing roster optimization models primarily rely on individual player ratings and aggregate performance statistics, which provide limited information about how players’ offensive contributions vary with their teammates. Recent advances in player-tracking technology have enabled statistical analyses of spatial shooting patterns, but these insights have rarely informed roster construction. We bridge this gap by developing a data-driven, risk-averse two-stage stochastic optimization framework for NBA roster construction. We first develop a Bayesian modeling framework that combines player statistics and spatial shot-chart data to identify player roles and estimate how teammate composition influences shot selection, shooting frequency, and scoring efficiency. The resulting model provides uncertainty-quantified offensive values for hypothetical five-player lineups, including combinations that have never played together. We then formulate roster construction as a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program that optimizes player acquisitions under NBA salary-cap regulations while allowing lineup playing-time allocations to adapt to uncertain player roles. We evaluate the framework using 240 team-offseason decisions over eight seasons and two additional held-out seasons. The results demonstrate that incorporating spatial shooting compatibility substantially changes optimal roster decisions and improves predicted offensive performance relative to approaches based on individual player values. We further find that flexibility in allocating playing time across lineups absorbs much of the uncertainty about player roles.

entry.title: Geary-type expectation identities for Mardia’s sample skewness and kurtosis

link.title: Geary-type expectation identities for Mardia’s sample skewness and kurtosis

entry.content: Under multivariate normality, we establish exact Geary-type expectation identities for Mardia’s sample skewness and kurtosis. A polar decomposition of the centered Gaussian data matrix shows that each of these statistics is independent of the sample covariance matrix. This independence allows the moments of each statistic to be expressed as ratios of expectations involving polynomial numerators and powers of the determinant of the sample covariance matrix. The identities hold in arbitrary dimension $p$. To illustrate their use, we give exact expressions for the variance of Mardia’s sample skewness and the third central moment of Mardia’s sample kurtosis for $p=2$ and $p=3$. As an application of the exact variance formulas, we construct a moment-matched chi-square approximation to the null distribution of Mardia’s sample skewness and compare its performance with Mardia’s classical and mean-corrected approximations.

entry.title: Fairness-Regularized Principal Component Analysis

link.title: Fairness-Regularized Principal Component Analysis

entry.content: Principal component analysis (PCA) optimizes aggregate reconstruction accuracy but may represent heterogeneous groups unevenly. We study fairness-regularized PCA, which balances aggregate reconstruction risk against worst-group reconstruction regret, and establish its population and statistical properties. First, we characterize the reconstruction-fairness trade-off and show that, under a nondegeneracy condition, a small fairness penalty reduces worst-group regret to first order while increasing aggregate reconstruction risk only to second order. This reveals a vanishing initial marginal cost of improving fairness. We also identify conditions under which the regularization path remains locally constant. A minimax spectral characterization shows that, under an optimal effective eigengap condition, the convex relaxation is exact and Fair PCA is equivalent to ordinary PCA with endogenously adjusted group weights. Second, we develop a statistical theory for estimating fairness-regularized principal subspaces. A uniform eigengap over the set of possibly nonunique dual optimizers implies polyhedral identification and quadratic growth, yielding first-order perturbation bounds and convergence rates that accommodate growing dimensions, ranks, and numbers of groups. Third, we establish uniform recovery of the reconstruction-fairness path and theoretical guarantees for data-adaptive penalty selection. Simulations and an NHANES accelerometry application demonstrate substantial improvements in worst-group representation quality with minimal loss of aggregate reconstruction accuracy.

entry.title: Simple, general strategies for correcting the upward bias of calibration summaries of prediction models

link.title: Simple, general strategies for correcting the upward bias of calibration summaries of prediction models

entry.content: For clinical prediction models, calibration across the spectrum of predicted values is often assessed via flexible calibration curves and associated scalar summaries such as the integrated calibration index (ICI). However, these scalar summaries tend to have a finite-sample upward bias, as they are based on the absolute value of an estimate whose sampling distribution can cross zero. We show the mechanism underlying this bias and quantify its magnitude as a function of the true calibration error and its variance. This mechanism motivates easily implementable methods for reducing the bias (plug-in and inversion methods, each applied locally or globally) that are applicable to any smoothing method that generates an estimate and its sampling variance for each point on the calibration curve. These methods are general in that 1) they can be used for different outcome types (continuous, binary, time-to-event, as well as counterfactual outcomes for models that predict treatment benefit), and 2) the resulting bias-adjusted calibration error curves yield bias-corrected estimates of other metrics such as quantile-based ones (e.g., E50 and E90). Focusing on ICI as an exemplary metric, numerical and case studies demonstrate that the upward bias can be substantial, especially when the sample is small and the true ICI is close to zero. Results show that the Global Inversion method removed the most bias, particularly when the bias was substantial, although it could slightly increase the mean absolute error if the bias was small.

entry.title: Certifying a Sufficient Gaussian Dependence Regime for Learned Weighted FDR Control

link.title: Certifying a Sufficient Gaussian Dependence Regime for Learned Weighted FDR Control

entry.content: Learning hypothesis weights from informative auxiliary data can improve the power of multiple testing. Even when the weights are learned independently of the tests, the validity of weighted Benjamini-Hochberg depends on their joint distribution. We use reference observations to certify a sufficient dependence condition for one-sided Gaussian tests. An intersection-union test of uncertain correlation signs determines whether to apply weighted Benjamini-Hochberg or a prespecified fallback at an adjusted level. Under conditional separation of certification and testing, the procedure controls the false discovery rate (FDR) for every Gaussian correlation matrix satisfying the stated sampling assumptions and weight constraints. We establish a boundary obstruction to uniform certification and matching minimax sample-size bounds for worst-case pair sets and the all-pairs problem. In the parameter ranges of the matching bounds, the minimax sample size grows logarithmically with the number of checked pairs and quadratically with the inverse of their positive margin. For homogeneous Gaussian observations with known marginal variances, residual contrasts from the testing subjects provide an independent source of certification scores. Simulations with up to 4,950 checked pairs, comparisons under a common subject budget, and Gaussian designs based on correlations estimated from the Healthy Brain Network illustrate the trade-off between certification and detection power.

entry.title: The Illusion of an Automated German Census: Assessing the Feasibility of the 2031 Register-Based Census via Simulation

link.title: The Illusion of an Automated German Census: Assessing the Feasibility of the 2031 Register-Based Census via Simulation

entry.content: The next German Census (2031) is planned to be the country’s first fully register-based census, relying exclusively on administrative data sources. In addition to the population registers, ten further administrative registers are envisaged, covering a wide range of information, from driving licences to agricultural social insurance. This study simulates potential data-quality challenges in linking these registers using quasi-identifiers (QIDs), such as names and dates of birth. Using a synthetic population dataset (N=80,206,770), we systematically vary experimental factors related to register characteristics. Across the 1,458 experimental conditions studied, results vary considerably. Some plausible scenarios range from 500,000 to 1,000,000 false-negative linkage errors per linked register. These findings suggest that implementing an automated register-based census using the currently envisaged registers may prove challenging and could require substantial manual post-processing to achieve acceptable data quality.

entry.title: Nonparametric predictive inference for interval-censored data: M-functions anchored to the self-consistent estimator

link.title: Nonparametric predictive inference for interval-censored data: M-functions anchored to the self-consistent estimator

entry.content: Nonparametric predictive inference specifies the distribution of a future observation through M-functions, which are basic probability assignments on intervals. Here such a specification is proposed for data censored on the left, on the right or within intervals of arbitrary width. It is the union of two M-functions. The first rests on a post-data assumption under which each censored observation divides its predictive mass equally amongst the observations with regions inside its own, and it reproduces the right-censored theory exactly. The second combines the Turnbull estimator with one unconstrained unit of predictive mass. The resulting survival bounds contain the Turnbull estimator, lie inside the bounds from all completions of the data and need no enumeration. In simulated inspection schemes they were calibrated for fixed events and for the rank of a further observation, while the second member alone was not. Equal weights on all orderings allowed by the data give the first member whenever the regions are nested or disjoint. The method is compared with the Turnbull estimator on two interval-censored studies.

entry.title: Design-based causal inference for ROC curves

link.title: Design-based causal inference for ROC curves

entry.content: In randomized experiments, causal inference traditionally focuses on the average treatment effect, yet comparing the treatment and control potential outcome distributions is often of interest. Under complete randomization, we adopt a design-based framework without imposing an outcome model to study the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which measures the proportion of treated outcomes exceeding each upper quantile of the control distribution. We propose an estimator that depends only on pooled outcome ranks, establish its asymptotic normality, and construct conservative variance estimators and confidence intervals. We also develop covariate adjustment directly for the ROC estimator, preserving the target estimand while achieving an asymptotic variance no larger than that of the unadjusted estimator. We further construct simultaneous confidence bands over an interior range of quantile levels and extend pointwise inference to the extreme upper tail of the control distribution, with both extensions accommodating covariate adjustment. Simulation studies and an application to a large-scale online learning experiment illustrate the proposed methods.

entry.title: Gaussian Process Stochastic Frontiers with Two-Way Fixed Effects

link.title: Gaussian Process Stochastic Frontiers with Two-Way Fixed Effects

entry.content: Parametric frontier restrictions and unobserved time heterogeneity can distort efficiency measurement in panel data. This paper develops a Bayesian stochastic frontier model with a Gaussian process prior and unrestricted individual and time effects that may be correlated with inputs. Conditional on inefficiency, orthogonal projection eliminates both sets of fixed effects, yielding a restricted likelihood that retains observation-specific inefficiency. Monte Carlo experiments show competitive performance under correct parametric specification and improved performance when benchmark models impose an incorrect frontier functional form or omit time effects. An application to Spanish dairy farms observed from 1999 to 2010 yields similar average technical efficiency across specifications, but a lower posterior mean of average returns to scale, with greater uncertainty, under the Gaussian process frontier. Models with year effects also yield more stable estimated efficiency profiles than the benchmark with a quadratic trend and time-input interactions. These findings show that conclusions about scale economies and efficiency dynamics depend on both frontier flexibility and the treatment of time heterogeneity.

entry.title: Beyond Gentrification: quantifying the economic, social and cultural dimensions of neighbourhood change through housing markets and digital traces

link.title: Beyond Gentrification: quantifying the economic, social and cultural dimensions of neighbourhood change through housing markets and digital traces

entry.content: Neighbourhood change is a multidimensional process in which economic, demographic, social and cultural transformations do not necessarily coincide over space and time. However, data driven approaches typically collapse these into single indices or regression models, losing the nuances of individual components. This paper integrates housing market, demographic and social media data (SMD) to characterise different configurations of neighbourhood change in Leeds and Bradford, UK. Rates of change (2014-2019) were estimated over Lower Super Output Areas for house prices relative to the 250 nearest neighbouring areas, and for residential mobility, ethnic composition, unemployment and professional occupation. Approximately 1.6 million geo-tagged tweets, filtered for personal users using a large language model (LLM), were analysed using Structural Topic Models with socio-economic prevalence covariates, LLM based neighbourhood characterisation and text embeddings scored against gentrification and decline archetypes. These measures were used as inputs to a model-based cluster analysis, which identified six distinct neighbourhood types, and a spatially varying multinomial GAM was used to examine the effects of changes in the inputs on cluster membership. The results show repeated divergence between structural and discursive trajectories: rapid turnover that is invisible in local SMD discourse, heritage villages experiencing amenity and incomer pressure, a settled British-Pakistani community whose stability would be mis-characterised as stagnation or decline, and marginal areas accumulating strain with little on-line signal. This suggests that SMD derived measures can provide independent information on neighbourhood character rather than simply confirming structural indicators, although low SMD signals may reflect under-detection rather than an absence of change.

entry.title: Permutation tests for Poisson network regression: Double semi-partialling, studentized statistics and actor effects

link.title: Permutation tests for Poisson network regression: Double semi-partialling, studentized statistics and actor effects

entry.content: The multiple regression quadratic assignment procedure (MRQAP) is a standard framework for inference on dyadic network data, and its properties are well established for the linear model. Network outcomes are often counts, modelled by Poisson regression with a log link. We prove that the invariance property of the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, the only part that double semi-partialling (DSP) requires, survives the nonlinear link. The DSP focal coefficient and its model-based, HC3 and dyadic cluster-robust standard errors coincide with those of the fit on the raw covariates. The choice between relabelling the raw focal array ($X$-permutation) and relabelling its DSP residual acts only on the reference distribution. The test holds its level when the relabelled designs reproduce the dependence that the statistic retains, and DSP reproduces the autocorrelation of the partialled focal covariate. When the raw focal array and its residual share their autocorrelation, the relabelling test holds the nominal level for all three statistics, at covariate correlations up to $0.9$ and in networks of $20$ to $100$ actors. A normal reference rejects a true null at rates up to $0.96$. With sender and receiver effects modelled, every statistic rejects a true null at $0.035$ to $0.070$ in all conditions, and power against a focal effect of $0.10$ rises from at most $32\%$ to at least $99.9\%$. When the actor effects cannot be modelled, adding the sender and receiver means of the nuisance covariates keeps DSP at its level. We give recommendations and illustrate the method on the EIES message-count network.

entry.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective

link.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective

entry.content: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

entry.title: Pseudo-IPD Reconstruction from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves under Unidentified Within-Interval Censoring

link.title: Pseudo-IPD Reconstruction from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves under Unidentified Within-Interval Censoring

entry.content: Reconstruction of pseudo-individual patient data (pseudo-IPD) from published Kaplan-Meier curves and number-at-risk tables is widely used to support secondary survival analyses when individual-level data are unavailable. However, the reconstruction is generally not unique because the published information does not determine how censoring is distributed within each risk-table interval. We study the non-identifiability that remains after interval-level event and censoring totals have been reconstructed. Different within-interval censoring placements can yield similarly good Kaplan-Meier agreement but different risk-set and censoring patterns, with possible effects on subsequent analyses. We characterize this non-identifiability, introduce a systematic allocation scheme, and assess its impact on reconstructed pseudo-IPD and downstream analyses. Simulation studies were conducted to examine how within-interval censoring allocation affects pseudo-IPD reconstruction under different risk-table resolutions and censoring settings. The proposed approach was also illustrated using published data from CheckMate 067. Our analysis suggests that considering multiple reconstructions provides a practical way to assess the impact of this non-identifiability on downstream analyses.

link.title: Guarded Readmission Weighting for Robust Single-Index Frechet Regression

entry.content: Single-index Frechet regression reduces the predictor dimension for metric-space responses such as distributions, networks or curves, but its estimators are sensitive to outliers. We propose guarded readmission weighting (GRW), a one-step computation of case weights from the predictors and the response distances, usable with any weighted estimator. GRW starts from a high-breakdown fit to a multidimensional scaling surrogate, readmits cases by an add-one metric Cook’s distance, downweights remote predictors and keeps a response isolation factor in the final weights. If fewer than $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of the $n$ cases are replaced, objects far from the uncontaminated responses receive weight zero; under elliptical predictors, weights depending on the predictors only through the index and the Mahalanobis distance keep the population weighted directions in the index subspace. In simulations, three GRW-weighted estimators keep the mean projection distance to the true direction below about 0.5 under up to 30% scattered and 20% clustered bad leverage points, whereas deletion and $\alpha$-distance covariance become much less accurate as contamination grows; $\alpha$-distance covariance is more accurate in most clean, shape-outlier and good-leverage settings. In two applications, under planted contamination, the weighted surrogate-assisted and least squares directions move less than those of methods without GRW.

entry.title: BADGERS: Bayesian Adaptive Graph-Guided Errors-in-Variables Regression Solution for Structured High-Dimensional Data

link.title: BADGERS: Bayesian Adaptive Graph-Guided Errors-in-Variables Regression Solution for Structured High-Dimensional Data

entry.content: Knowledge-guided learning methods that incorporate biological graph information into the analysis of structured high-dimensional data, such as genomic data, can improve variable selection and prediction accuracy while yielding more interpretable results. However, these methods typically assume that covariates are measured without error. This assumption is often violated in omics studies involving replicated measurements. To address this gap, we develop the Bayesian Adaptive Graph-guided Errors-in-variables Regression Solution (BADGERS), a Bayesian framework that jointly accounts for covariate measurement error and incorporates graph information while accommodating varying numbers of replicates across covariates. BADGERS treats the true covariates as latent variables and integrates three key components: a Gaussian errors-in-variables model using replicated measurements to inform the latent true covariates, a Bayesian adaptive graphical lasso with a graph-informed prior to model their dependence structure, and a regression model with an adaptive structured shrinkage prior to leverage graph information and facilitate variable selection. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior sampling. We demonstrate the advantages of BADGERS over existing methods through simulation studies and analyses of gene expression datasets for Alzheimer’s disease and multiple myeloma.

entry.title: The Last Expectation: Sampling Measurement Outcomes in Value of Information Analysis

link.title: The Last Expectation: Sampling Measurement Outcomes in Value of Information Analysis

entry.content: In decision-making under uncertainty, additional information can improve decisions but is often costly to acquire. The Value of Information (VoI) quantifies the expected benefit of different information-gathering strategies. The main computational burden in VoI analysis arises from evaluating the expected utility of a strategy over possible outcomes. As each outcome entails solving a computationally expensive optimization problem under uncertainty to determine the optimal decision, efficient estimation of this expectation is crucial. This work focuses on sampling-based estimation and investigates three classical variance-reduction techniques, namely control variates, stratified sampling, and importance sampling, as well as combinations thereof. In particular, we establish a connection between two common VoI formulations through a control variate framework and show how this relationship can be exploited to obtain more efficient VoI estimators. The methodology is assessed using three test cases. The first is an analytical example with a known reference solution, the second involves a fatigue reliability and the third a slope stability application. Our results demonstrate that the relative performance of the sampling methods depends strongly on the problem characteristics. However, suitable combinations of variance-reduction techniques consistently improve efficiency and provide stable VoI estimates across a range of scenarios.

entry.title: Analytical Wald Power for Lagged Coefficients in the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model

link.title: Analytical Wald Power for Lagged Coefficients in the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model

entry.content: In a longitudinal study, the number of participants and the number of waves both affect how much power the study has to detect a lagged effect. The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) is widely used to study within-person dynamics, but existing approaches to power analysis for this model typically rely on simulation or target likelihood-ratio tests. Starting from the likelihood score, we derive analytical Wald power for each lagged coefficient in the bivariate RI-CLPM. Across 30 designs, we compared our analytical results with power estimates from two R packages, powRICLPM for simulated Wald power and semPower for analytical likelihood-ratio power. The mean absolute difference was less than one percentage point in each comparison. By avoiding repeated simulation and model fitting, the analytical method saves time when evaluating power for a target path across many combinations of sample size (N) and number of waves (T).

entry.title: Projection of multidimensional count data IRT models and their empirical indistinguishability

link.title: Projection of multidimensional count data IRT models and their empirical indistinguishability

entry.content: Empirical test data is rarely unidimensional. If one dimension is of interest, projective item-response-theory (IRT) models can be used to work with a unidimensional model without neglecting the multidimensionality of the data. This work extends the projective IRT literature to count data IRT models from the Two-Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model framework. We build on the definition of empirical indistinguishability and analytically derive closed-form expressions for discrimination parameters and item intercepts after projection. The dispersion parameters of the projected Two- Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model are obtained with numerical approximations. The analytical calculations are not limited to the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson distribution. In addition, rotation methods are applied before projection. Results are illustrated and evaluated using empirical data from cognitive ability assessment items and in a simulation study. The projected model performed better in terms of RMSE, Spearman correlation between the true and estimated person parameters, and coverage of 95% confidence intervals based on the Fisher information than an approximation by a standard unidimensional model fitted to multidimensional data. No improvement in bias over the standard unidimensional model, nor improvement across all metrics over the multidimensional model, were observed.

entry.title: The Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model: A Semi-mechanistic Generative Model for Temporal Hypergraphs

link.title: The Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model: A Semi-mechanistic Generative Model for Temporal Hypergraphs

entry.content: Many complex networks involve time-varying relations between more than two nodes. Such networks are naturally modeled by temporal hypergraphs. We propose the Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model (HHCM), a semi-mechanistic model for temporal hypergraphs that combines a Hawkes process to model the timestamps of hyperedges with a noisy copy mechanism to model the nodes present in hyperedges. Each hyperedge is either generated as an exogenous event with a baseline rate or an endogenous event as a noisy copy of a previous hyperedge. Our proposed model can be used for credit attribution, where the objective is to quantify the influence or contribution of a prior hyperedge to a current one. We apply the HHCM to perform attribution on several real network datasets with higher-order relations, including email networks and militarized interstate dispute networks.

entry.title: Minimising sample size across analysis strategies in preclinical research: Reduced power or negligible benefit

link.title: Minimising sample size across analysis strategies in preclinical research: Reduced power or negligible benefit

entry.content: Preclinical animal studies often allow multiple valid statistical analysis strategies, which can result in different sample sizes required to achieve a target power. Because reducing animal use is an ethical, financial, and practical priority, researchers have a clear incentive to choose the strategy requiring the fewest animals. This may, however, favour an overly optimistic estimate of the sample size required, particularly when prior information is uncertain or biased. This study investigates how minimising sample size across analysis strategies affects statistical power and animal use. We conceptualise this practice as sample size hacking, describe its underlying mechanism, and evaluate its consequences using a simulation study based on a real preclinical cancer study. We varied effect sizes, the level of uncertainty in prior information, and the degree of follow-up bias to assess the resulting sample size reductions and achieved statistical power. Sample size minimisation across analysis strategies substantially reduced the achieved statistical power in several scenarios, particularly for moderate effect sizes and greater uncertainty in prior information. For larger effect sizes or in the presence of follow-up bias, the impact on power was less pronounced, but the resulting reduction in sample size was also smaller. Selecting an analysis strategy solely because it yields the smallest calculated sample size may in fact compromise statistical power, while offering only limited animal savings in other settings. These findings underscore the importance of justifying and pre-specifying the analysis strategy before sample size planning to limit potentially problematic analytical flexibility, reduce the risk of underpowered studies, and promote transparency in preclinical research.

entry.title: The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model as a Statistical Model: Identification, Estimation, and Model Comparison

link.title: The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model as a Statistical Model: Identification, Estimation, and Model Comparison

entry.content: The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) distinguishes stable differences between people from lagged associations within individuals. We use a matrix representation to study its statistical properties for p variables measured across T waves. We derive a necessary and sufficient rank condition for global identification when transition matrices and innovation covariances vary by wave. Under time-invariant transitions, the condition specifies when three waves suffice. For complete Gaussian trajectories, matrix differentiation yields the profile likelihood score for each covariance and transition block. We also derive the population parameters of the conventional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) when an RI-CLPM with fixed parameters generates the data. Our formulas quantify how CLPM slopes for observed variables differ from RI-CLPM slopes for within-person deviations at each transition. When the RI-CLPM transition matrix is time-invariant, the comparison also covers CLPM slopes pooled across waves. The formulas recover earlier bivariate results and show when cross-lagged slopes can appear, cancel, reverse sign, or change their ordering across models.

entry.title: Who Fills the Gap? Role Similarity and Teammates’ Minutes When NBA Players Are Ruled Out

link.title: Who Fills the Gap? Role Similarity and Teammates’ Minutes When NBA Players Are Ruled Out

entry.content: When a core player is ruled out before an NBA game, do teammates whose statistical role resembles that of the removed set (every rotation player ruled out, about three per case) play more? Using injury reports stamped at least six hours before tip-off and rosters reconstructed after the season, we study 2,441 team-games from 2023-24 to 2025-26 in which a core player was ruled out for a medical reason. Among teammates in the same game, one within-case standard deviation more similarity in role profile (three-point attempts, assists and rebounds per minute) goes with about 0.63 more minutes, holding reference minutes and headroom fixed (p < 0.0001); this compares teammates within a game, not the minutes gained because of the absence. The pattern holds in two earlier seasons and in exploratory within-player and without-and-with comparisons. Whether similarity adds to listed position is not settled. The association is small and yielded no statistically detectable reduction in the error of the retrospective minute forecasts we tested. Role coverage, how much of the missing minutes and roles the remaining rotation could restore, showed no consistent incremental association with team role output or the final margin.

entry.title: ENSO-linked redistribution of post-monsoon tropical cyclone energy between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal: 1982–2025

link.title: ENSO-linked redistribution of post-monsoon tropical cyclone energy between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal: 1982–2025

entry.content: Tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean (NIO) form in two sub-basins, the Arabian Sea (AS) and the Bay of Bengal (BoB), which are usually studied separately, with their relationship to the El Ni~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) treated as stationary. We develop a joint inter-basin statistical framework and apply it to 416 disturbances from quality-controlled IBTrACS best tracks for 1982–2025, with harmonised IMD and JTWC intensities, ERA5 and ERSSTv5. The framework tests whether ENSO changes the basin total or redistributes energy between the sub-basins, separates its effect on formation from that on intensification, attributes each sub-basin’s response to environmental terms along individual tracks, and tests stationarity and the record length needed to detect trends. In October-December, ENSO redistributes rather than changes the total: for a one-standard-deviation increase in Ni~no-3.4 (about 1 $^\circ$C), accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) is multiplied by 1.89 in the AS and by 0.63 in the BoB, while the NIO total shows no detectable change (factor 0.99 [0.74, 1.32]). ENSO acts on intensification, with no detectable effect on formation: the odds that a cyclonic storm becomes very severe rise about fourfold in the AS and halve in the BoB, through lower vertical wind shear (VWS) over the AS and weaker low-level vorticity over the BoB. The relationship has changed: El Ni~no lowered total NIO energy in 1982–2003, but in 2004-2025 AS gains balanced BoB losses (change p = 0.016). Very severe storms and rapid intensification increased in the AS only, and no 15-year window detects this increase, so about three decades of data are needed. The post-monsoon IOD signal can hardly be separated from ENSO, and August Ni~no-3.4 gives modest skill for the AS-BoB partition but none for the basin total.

entry.title: Modeling time series of high-resolution spectra using the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition with application to radial velocity exoplanet searches

link.title: Modeling time series of high-resolution spectra using the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition with application to radial velocity exoplanet searches

entry.content: We describe a framework for building low-rank separable expansions to model spectroscopic data from systems with time-varying spectra, in settings where the spectral dimension is finely sampled (in wavelength), but the temporal dimension is sparsely and possibly irregulary sampled. The motivating application is detection and characterization of small exoplanets, e.g., Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. Such planets cannot be seen directly, but can be detected via the minute Doppler shifts of the host star spectrum due to the star’s motion as the planet and star revolve around their mutual center of mass. Current instruments are reaching the precision necessary to detect the ~10 cm/s motions corresponding to an exo-Earth. But the small Doppler shifts from such low-amplitude orbital motion can be masked or mimicked by the effects of stellar activity on the surface of the host star. e.g., starspots (dark regions), faculae (bright filaments), etc. One technique astronomers have used to try to model the stellar activity component of the signal is PCA, applied to an ensemble of spectra collected over time. But PCA neglects the continuous function nature of a spectrum at a given time, and the continuous evolution of spectra over time. We address model building from a function approximation perspective, via the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition (HSD). This provides a PCA-like low-rank decomposition of a dynamic spectrum, but it explicitly accounts for time dependence, both estimating temporal basis functions, and accounting for irregular temporal sampling when estimating spectral basis functions. We show that HSD improves the fidelity of a fixed-order model of the dynamic spectrum of a Sun-like star with a starspot, with mean squared error for spectral basis functions many times smaller than achieved via PCA when spectra are randomly sampled sparsely and irregularly in time.

entry.title: PrO Filtering via Kernel Mean Embedding Dynamics

link.title: PrO Filtering via Kernel Mean Embedding Dynamics

entry.content: Filtering methods are routinely deployed with misspecified state-space models, where Bayesian filters can diverge and become overconfident. Predictively-oriented (PrO) filtering is a recent, hyperparameter-free alternative that was demonstrated to outperform (generalised) Bayesian filtering methods when either the dynamical model or the measurement model is structurally misspecified. This can be attributed to \emph{hedging} behaviour: when an observation conflicts with the forecast, the PrO update places mass near both. Yet existing implementations of PrO filtering rely on unimodal (Gaussian) approximations, whose ability to effectively hedge is limited. This paper develops the first nonparametric, particle-based implementation of PrO filtering. The key obstacle, that PrO filtering distributions are only implicitly defined, is overcome by constructing a path from the predictive to the PrO filtering distribution whose rate is available in closed form, enabling the use of kernel mean embedding dynamics for measure transport. The resulting algorithm requires only simulation from the dynamical model and evaluations of the likelihood, with neither importance weights nor the predictive density. Moreover, as we prove, the number of pseudo-time steps it requires does not grow with the outlyingness of the observation, in contrast to transport along the Bayesian tempering path. An empirical assessment shows substantial improvement over Gaussian variation of PrO filtering in challenging nonlinear examples where Gaussian approximation is unreasonably limited.

entry.title: Atheism and Cross-Country National Cognitive Skills: Evidence from a Beta Regression Analysis

link.title: Atheism and Cross-Country National Cognitive Skills: Evidence from a Beta Regression Analysis

entry.content: This study performs a beta regression analysis to investigate how country-level cognitive skills—measured using harmonized large-scale international educational assessments and expressed on an IQ-type scale—are associated with the prevalence of atheism in 131 countries. We find that this association is nonlinear: at low levels of cognitive skills, increases are associated with lower expected levels of atheism, whereas beyond a threshold, they are associated with higher expected atheism rates. This turning point is estimated to occur at approximately 65 on the IQ-type scale. The strength and location of the relationship vary across regions. We estimate elasticities of expected atheism rates with respect to cognitive skills for all countries in the sample and introduce the concept of the atheism gap to identify countries where observed prevalence is substantially higher or lower than predicted by their conditioning variables.

entry.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning

link.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning

entry.content: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of “elsewhere” is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model’s resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.

entry.title: Measurement Errors in Semiparametric Generalized Regression Models

link.title: Measurement Errors in Semiparametric Generalized Regression Models

entry.content: Regression models that ignore measurement error in predictors may produce highly biased estimates leading to erroneous inferences. It is well known that it is extremely difficult to take measurement error into account in Gaussian nonparametric regression. This problem becomes tremendously more difficult when considering other families such as logistic regression, Poisson and negative-binomial. For the first time, we present a method aiming to correct for measurement error when estimating regression functions flexibly covering virtually all distributions and link functions regularly considered in generalized linear models. This approach depends on approximating the first and the second moment of the response after integrating out the true unobserved predictors in a semiparametric generalized linear model. Unlike previous methods, this method is not restricted to truncated splines and can utilize various basis functions. Through extensive simulation studies, we study the performance of our method under many scenarios.

entry.title: Visualizing the geometry of labeled high-dimensional data with spheres

link.title: Visualizing the geometry of labeled high-dimensional data with spheres

entry.content: Data visualizations can summarize high-dimensional distributions in two or three dimensions. Dimensionality reduction entails a loss of information, and what is preserved differs between methods. Existing methods preserve the local or the global geometry of the points, and most techniques do not consider labels. Here we introduce “hypersphere2sphere” (H2S), a new method that aims to visualize not the points, but the relationships between the labeled distributions. H2S fits a hypersphere to each labeled set of points in the high-dimensional space of the original data and visualizes each hypersphere as a sphere in 3D (or a circle in 2D). H2S perfectly captures the geometry of up to 4 high-dimensional hyperspheres using spheres in 3D (or 3 using circles in 2D), and approximates the geometry for larger numbers of distributions, matching the sizes (radii), and the pairwise separations (between-center distances) and the overlaps (along the center-connection line). The resulting visualizations are robust to sampling imbalances. Leveraging labels and the sphere as the simplest geometrical primitive, H2S provides an important addition to the toolbox of visualization techniques.

entry.title: Treatment Effects in Extreme Regimes

link.title: Treatment Effects in Extreme Regimes

entry.content: Understanding treatment effects in extreme regimes is important for characterizing risks associated with different interventions. This is hindered by the unavailability of counterfactual outcomes and the rarity and difficulty of collecting extreme data in practice. To address this issue, we propose a new framework based on extreme value theory for estimating treatment effects in extreme regimes. We quantify these effects using variations in tail decay rates of potential outcomes in the presence and absence of treatments. We establish algorithms for calculating these quantities and develop related theoretical results. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on various standard synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets.

entry.title: On importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings with an unbounded weight function

link.title: On importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings with an unbounded weight function

entry.content: Importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings are among the fundamental building blocks of Monte Carlo methods. Both require a proposal distribution that globally approximates the target distribution, and pointwise evaluation of the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the target distribution relative to the proposal, also called the weight function. We study the bias of importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings, without assuming that the weight function is bounded. We show that the common random numbers coupling of independent Metropolis-Hastings is maximal. Using that coupling, we derive polynomial bounds on the total variation distance of the chain to its target distribution. We further consider bias removal techniques using couplings, and provide conditions under which the resulting unbiased estimators have finite moments, and under which their efficiency is comparable to that of importance sampling. Experiments illustrate unbiased estimators of the inverse of a normalizing constant, estimators of nested expectations, and combination of importance sampling with robust mean estimation methods.

entry.title: Spatiotemporal Causal Inference with Spillover and Carryover Effects: Airstrikes and Insurgent Violence in Vietnam and Afghanistan

link.title: Spatiotemporal Causal Inference with Spillover and Carryover Effects: Airstrikes and Insurgent Violence in Vietnam and Afghanistan

entry.content: Do airstrikes suppress insurgent violence or provoke it? Answering such questions requires methods that preserve the spatial and temporal structure of airstrikes and insurgent retaliation. Yet nearly all microlevel research aggregates fine-grained data into panels built on large administrative units and long time intervals. This practice forecloses direct tests of causal mechanisms and imposes restrictive assumptions about spillover and carryover that bias estimates. We develop a practical framework for spatiotemporal causal inference in which treatment, mediator, and outcome all retain their precise locations and timing. Applying it to declassified airstrike data from Vietnam and Afghanistan, we find that bombing displaces, but does not suppress, insurgent violence. Insurgent retaliation follows predictable patterns, concentrating near rebel-controlled hamlets (Vietnam) and U.S. bases (Afghanistan) and emerging about a week later. Civilian harm does not mediate this response. Post-airstrike insurgent violence appears less about avenging aggrieved civilians than demonstrating resolve by imposing costs on counterinsurgents.

entry.title: Sequential Monte Carlo approximations of Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao gradient flows

link.title: Sequential Monte Carlo approximations of Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao gradient flows

entry.content: We consider the problem of sampling from a probability distribution $\pi$. It is well known that this can be written as an optimisation problem over the space of probability distribution in which we aim to minimise the Kullback–Leibler divergence from $\pi$. We consider several partial differential equations (PDEs) whose solution is a minimiser of the Kullback–Leibler divergence from $\pi$ and connect them to well-known Monte Carlo algorithms. We focus in particular on PDEs obtained by considering the Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao geometry over the space of probabilities and show that these lead to a natural implementation using importance sampling and sequential Monte Carlo. We propose a novel algorithm to approximate the Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao flow of the Kullback–Leibler divergence and conduct an extensive empirical study to identify when this algorithm outperforms other popular Monte Carlo algorithms.

entry.title: Perfect Clustering in Extremely Sparse Multilayer Networks with Groupwise Subspace Structure

link.title: Perfect Clustering in Extremely Sparse Multilayer Networks with Groupwise Subspace Structure

entry.content: The paper studies a multilayer network on the same collection of nodes, where each layer follows the Generalized Random Dot Product Graph Model. Furthermore, all layers can be partitioned into groups, each group with its own unique latent subspace structure, but otherwise the matrices of connection probabilities can all be different. This setting is extremely general and includes most multilayer network models as special cases. In addition, we are interested in the situation where the layer networks may be extremely sparse and, therefore, the layer-by-layer analysis is unreliable. This problem can also be seen as a generalization of the classic setting in which one recovers a shared structure across an entire collection of matrices, extending it to the case where such structures are shared only within specific groups of matrices. The key task in this setting is to recover the groups of layers with unique subspace structures, since, after that, the information in those groups of layers can be pooled together by well-studied methods. Until now, clustering of layers in such networks was based on layer-by-layer analysis, which required the multilayer network to be sufficiently dense. Our paper is the first to provide a tensor-based approach to the problem that combines information from all layers in an unconventional manner. Our theoretical results, established under intuitive and non-restrictive assumptions, assert that the new technique achieves perfect clustering under sparsity conditions that, up to logarithmic factors, coincide with the computational lower bound derived for a much simpler model. The paper also delivers a nuanced message about the applicability of the new technique.

entry.title: Efficient Prediction of pass@k Scaling in Large Language Models

link.title: Efficient Prediction of pass@k Scaling in Large Language Models

entry.content: Assessing the capabilities and risks of frontier AI systems is a critical area of research; recent work has shown that repeated sampling can dramatically increase both. For instance, repeated sampling allows models to solve difficult math and coding problems, but it may also increase their risk of being jailbroken. Such results raise a crucial question: how can one accurately predict a model’s behavior when scaled to a massive number of attempts, given a vastly smaller sampling budget? This question is directly relevant to model providers, who serve hundreds of millions of users daily, and to governmental regulators, who seek to prevent harms. To answer this question, we make three contributions. First, we find that standard methods for fitting these laws suffer from statistical shortcomings that hinder predictions, especially in data-limited scenarios. Second, we remedy these shortcomings by introducing a robust estimation framework, which uses a beta-binomial distribution to generate more accurate predictions from limited data. Third, we propose a dynamic sampling strategy that allocates a greater budget to harder problems. Combined, these innovations enable more reliable prediction of rare risks and capabilities at a fraction of the computational cost.

entry.title: Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry

link.title: Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry

entry.content: Variational inference (VI) approximates a target density $p$ by the best match $q$ in a family $\mathcal Q$ of tractable distributions. The variational approximation is found by minimizing a divergence, most commonly the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence $\text{KL}(q   p)$, although other divergences can be considered. In practice, $p \notin \mathcal Q$ and so the optimal variational approximation is misspecified. Despite this misspecification, it was recently shown that the minimizer of $\text{KL}(q   p)$ is guaranteed to recover the mean in the presence of even symmetry and likewise the correlation matrix in the presence of elliptical symmetry for a log-concave target $p$. We extend this result in several directions. First, we relax the assumption of log-concavity and instead merely require $p$ to be unimodal, allowing for heavy-tailed targets. Second, we obtain guarantees for cases where $p$ exhibits symmetry along some but not all of its coordinates. These partial symmetries arise naturally in Bayesian hierarchical models, where the prior induces a challenging geometry but still possesses axes of symmetry. Third, we extend these guarantees to $f$-divergences, a broad class which includes the forward and reverse-KL divergences and the $\alpha$-divergences.

entry.title: Statistical Inference for Fuzzy Clustering

link.title: Statistical Inference for Fuzzy Clustering

entry.content: Clustering is a central tool in biomedical research for discovering heterogeneous patient subpopulations, where group boundaries are often diffuse rather than sharply separated. While soft clustering methods such as fuzzy $c$-means (FCM) allow mixed memberships, principled statistical inference for fuzzy clustering remains limited. We propose a weighted fuzzy $c$-means (WFCM) framework for settings with cluster-size imbalance. Cluster-specific weights $\mathbf{w}$ re-balance the classic FCM criterion to adjust the relative influence of clusters of unequal size, and we construct a normalized working density from the weighted objective with scale parameter $\sigma$ and fuzziness parameter $m$. Estimation is performed via FCM-style alternating initialization followed by numerical likelihood refinement; the intractable normalizing constant is approximated by importance sampling using a data-adaptive Gaussian-mixture as the proposal distribution. We further develop bootstrap-based confidence intervals. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, validate the method in simulations, and illustrate it on single-cell RNA-seq, Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), and TCGA-BRCA data. These applications illustrate uncertainty quantification and interpretable soft memberships, ranging from imbalanced cell populations to graded compatibility with AD-like and non-AD-like prototypes.

entry.title: Deriving Complete Constraints in Hidden Variable Models

link.title: Deriving Complete Constraints in Hidden Variable Models

entry.content: Hidden variable graphical models can sometimes imply constraints on the observable distribution that are more complex than simple conditional independence relations. These observable constraints can falsify assumptions of the model and can be used to constrain estimation procedures to improve statistical efficiency. Knowing the complete set of observable constraints is thus ideal, but this can be difficult to determine in many settings. In models with categorical observed variables and a joint distribution that is completely characterized by linear relations to the probabilities of unobservable response function variables, we develop a systematic method for deriving the complete set of observable constraints. We illustrate the method in several settings, including ones that imply both inequality and equality constraints.

entry.title: Differential Privacy for Network Connectedness Indices

link.title: Differential Privacy for Network Connectedness Indices

entry.content: Researchers increasingly use data on social and economic networks to study a range of social science questions, but releasing statistics derived from networks can raise significant privacy concerns. We show how to release network connectedness indices that quantify assortative mixing across node attributes under edge-adjacent differential privacy. Directly adding noise to connectedness indices based on global sensitivity can result in poor accuracy both because connectedness indices have high global sensitivity and because a single node’s attribute can potentially be an input to connectedness in thousands of cells, leading to poor composition. Our method, which is straightforward to apply, first randomizes node attributes, then analytically debiases downstream statistics, and finally adds noise to protect the presence or absence of individual edges. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimators for both discrete and continuous labels and show our method works well in simulations and on real networks with as few as 200 nodes collected by social scientists.

entry.title: Flexible Matrix Estimation with Side Information

link.title: Flexible Matrix Estimation with Side Information

entry.content: We introduce a flexible framework for high-dimensional matrix estimation to incorporate side information for both rows and columns. Existing approaches, such as inductive matrix completion, often impose restrictive structure—for example, an exact low-rank covariate interaction term, linear covariate effects, and limited ability to exploit components explained only by one side (row or column) or by neither—and frequently omit an explicit noise component. To address these limitations, we propose to decompose the underlying matrix as the sum of four complementary components: (possibly nonlinear) interaction between row and column characteristics; row characteristic-driven component, column characteristic-driven component, and residual low-rank structure unexplained by observed characteristics. By combining sieve-based projection with nuclear-norm penalization, each component can be estimated separately and these estimated components can then be aggregated to yield a final estimate. We derive Frobenius- and entrywise-norm convergence rates that demonstrate the robustness of our estimator across a broad range of model configurations with varying degrees of informativeness in the side information. We further extend the method to partially observed matrices under both missing-at-random and missing-not-at-random mechanisms, including block-missing patterns motivated by causal panel data. Simulations and a real-data application to tobacco sales show that leveraging side information improves imputation accuracy and can enhance treatment-effect estimation relative to standard low-rank and spectral-based alternatives.

link.title: Generalized win fraction regression for composite survival endpoints

entry.content: We propose a generalized win fraction regression framework for prioritized composite survival outcomes. The framework models the conditional win fraction through a chosen link function (including identity, logit, or probit), thereby accommodating multi-component time-to-event endpoints within a unified regression structure. To handle right censoring, we construct inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted estimating equations that target the win fraction as if censoring were absent. Under the identity link, regression parameters characterize covariate associations on the natural win fraction scale. Under the logit link, they characterize the log odds of winning – a new and complementary effect measure that treats ties as failures to win, imposing a more conservative standard than the win ratio or win odds. When there are no ties, the logit win fraction model reduces to proportional win fraction regression; moreover, the unweighted version of our estimating equations numerically coincides with the proportional win fraction point estimator regardless of ties. We establish large-sample properties of the proposed estimators and derive a consistent sandwich variance estimator that accounts for uncertainty from the estimated censoring weights. Extensive simulations examine finite-sample performance across link functions and censoring rates, and our method is illustrated through a reanalysis of the HF-ACTION clinical trial.

entry.title: Multispectral representation of Distributed Acoustic Sensing data: a framework for physically interpretable feature extraction and visualization

link.title: Multispectral representation of Distributed Acoustic Sensing data: a framework for physically interpretable feature extraction and visualization

entry.content: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) enables continuous monitoring of dynamic strain along tens of kilometres of optical fibre, generating massive datasets whose interpretation and automated analysis remain challenging. DAS data can be understood as a time-distance image array. However, the absence of standardised representation methods limits both the physical interpretability and the development of automated image-based analysis pipelines. This work introduces a systematic framework for visualisation and feature extraction of DAS data based on a multispectral signal representation. The approach decomposes strain-rate measurements into predefined frequency bands and produces band-limited energy images that describe the spatial and temporal distribution of acoustic energy across distinct spectral regimes. The framework is evaluated using DAS recordings containing fin whale and blue whale vocalisations. Three experiments are conducted to assess the approach: enhanced visualisation of bioacoustic signals, unsupervised clustering of acoustic patterns, and event detection using a convolutional neural network. The visualisation experiment shows that the multispectral representation allows for the simultaneous visualisation of sets of events that cannot be visualised using the strain amplitude representation. The unsupervised clustering experiment confirms that the multispectral representation yields class-discriminative feature spaces without requiring labelled data, enabling the automatic grouping of acoustically distinct event types. Finally, the use of multispectral composites as input of a ResNet-18 achieves an accuracy of 95.9% in whale vocalisation detection, demonstrating that the proposed representation provides an effective feature space for automated analysis.

entry.title: A Tutorial for Evaluating Cure Model Appropriateness

link.title: A Tutorial for Evaluating Cure Model Appropriateness

entry.content: In survival analysis, traditional models assume all individuals will eventually experience the event of interest. However, advances in therapeutics have led to multiple clinical contexts with potentially curative therapies, and in these contexts, certain individuals may never experience the event. Statisticians have developed cure models as a methodology to address this challenge. However, despite significant statistical advances in cure models, we have seen more limited uptake in biomedical applications, and we hypothesize that this reflects limited guidance on the appropriate application of cure models. Cure models require specific identifiability conditions for valid parameter estimation, and previous reports have demonstrated significant issues with the inappropriate application of cure models. Existing tutorials for cure models focus on model implementation and either assume or provide only limited guidance on whether cure modeling is appropriate for the given dataset. This tutorial addresses this gap by describing a systematic procedure that integrates clinical judgment, visual inspection of Kaplan-Meier curves, and quantitative evaluation. We provide a worked example using data from a randomized clinical trial in acute myeloid leukemia, and we also summarize findings from a series of other datasets of hematopoietic cell transplantation to suggest broad practical guidance for choosing to apply cure models. By systematically evaluating cure model appropriateness before fitting these models, researchers can achieve more reliable survival analysis and improved clinical decision-making.

entry.content: The problem of detecting new signals in the presence of an unknown background is ubiquitous in scientific discoveries and is especially prominent in the physical sciences. entry.title: Functional Characterization of Choice-Implied Subjective Time in Intertemporal Financial Decisions

link.title: Functional Characterization of Choice-Implied Subjective Time in Intertemporal Financial Decisions

entry.content: Intertemporal choice is usually summarized by a discount rate or a predefined parametric discount function, leaving differences in the shape of individual discounting over the horizon unobserved. This paper proposes a Functional Data Analysis framework that reconstructs, for each respondent, a choice-implied subjective-time trajectory $\tau_i(t)$ from monetary equivalence judgments collected at thirteen horizons between seven days and five years. The trajectories are analyzed through derivatives, functional principal component analysis and clustering of the component scores, compared with exponential, Weber-Fechner and Stevens benchmarks in sample and in a leave-one-horizon-out design, and related to an explicit subjective-time positioning task. A Monte Carlo study evaluates the recovery of trajectory shape and group structure. The empirical application uses an online multilingual survey with 141 respondents; 140 are eligible, 61 report the full future amount at every horizon and 19 provide profiles that do not determine a decreasing discount curve, leaving 60 identified trajectories. Parametric subjective-time models are competitive in predicting held-out judgments, while partitions based on their parameters do not reproduce the functional partition. No statistically detectable correspondence with the explicit positioning task is found.

entry.title: A Markov duration model with power-law decay via level-slope matching

link.title: A Markov duration model with power-law decay via level-slope matching

entry.content: We develop a two-dimensional Markov duration model with power-law rate decay and a flexible residual distribution. The two state variables specify the excitation level and decay scale of a single power-law rate curve, and each update matches the level and slope jumps of a power-law Hawkes intensity. Under a sufficient stability condition, a finite residual mean, and a positive continuous residual density, the state at event times is positive Harris recurrent and converges geometrically in total variation to a unique invariant distribution. With unit exponential residuals, the sufficient region contains every parameter value for which the matched Hawkes process is subcritical. We apply the model to E-mini S\&P 500 futures and NVDA midquote durations at several price-change thresholds. Flexible residual laws improve likelihood-based fit, and power-law decay lowers one-step negative log predictive scores relative to exponential decay. An autoregressive conditional duration model generally leaves less residual autocorrelation, while forecast rankings vary with the price threshold and evaluation criterion.

entry.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors

link.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors

entry.content: Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) estimates directed effective connectivity, while parametric empirical Bayes (PEB) supports group inference using subject-specific posterior summaries. Standard PEB relies on Gaussian models and continuous shrinkage, making it sensitive to atypical estimates and unable to distinguish negligible from nonzero effects. We develop a robust and sparse group-DCM extension combining a Student-$t$ likelihood with a spike-and-slab prior using a nonlocal product-moment (pMOM) slab. A normal–gamma representation of the Student-$t$ distribution yields weights that downweight atypical {whitened residual coordinates}. The pMOM slab vanishes at zero, sharpening coefficient selection and yielding inclusion probabilities. {We propagate first-level posterior uncertainty through block-covariance pre-whitening and use a multistart generalized expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm with conditional maximization for mode fitting, followed by parallel-tempering posterior integration for inclusion probabilities. A simulation study showed that Student-$t$ weighting supplied the main protection against contamination, while spike-and-slab regularization reduced fixed-threshold false selections. In an openly shared mixed-gambles fMRI application, we found mild heterogeneity, concentrated inclusion support on departures of all four diagonal self-inhibition scaling parameters from the SPM default, and close directional agreement with standard PEB implemented in Statistical Parametric Mapping.} Our framework therefore adds interpretable {whitened-coordinate} robustness diagnostics and sparse coefficient selection to hierarchical DCM while retaining first-level uncertainty.

entry.title: Beyond Point Forecasts: A Survey on Probabilistic Forecasting for Time Series and Spatiotemporal Data

link.title: Beyond Point Forecasts: A Survey on Probabilistic Forecasting for Time Series and Spatiotemporal Data

entry.content: Probabilistic forecasting is central to decision-making under uncertainty, yet its methodological landscape has become increasingly fragmented across temporal and spatiotemporal forecasting, statistical modeling, machine learning, and deep generative modeling. This survey develops a unified perspective by organizing probabilistic forecasting methods according to where and how uncertainty is introduced into the forecasting pipeline. Our taxonomy connects model-agnostic approaches including ensembles and distribution-free calibration, with model-intrinsic approaches spanning Bayesian modeling, parametric predictive distributions, distributional regression, and modern generative models, and further examines the emerging role of time series foundation models. Beyond methodological synthesis, we identify the assumptions, computational demands, and forms of uncertainty represented by different paradigms, and translate these distinctions into data-driven and domain-specific guidance for method selection. We complement the survey with a cross-paradigm empirical study on univariate, multivariate, and spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. The results reveal that no single uncertainty-quantification paradigm dominates across settings. Calibration, sharpness, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency can lead to substantially different model preferences, while expressive generative models and zero-shot foundation models exhibit markedly different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Lastly, we identify unresolved challenges surrounding uncertainty in evolving dependency structures, physics-informed predictive distributions, forecasting extreme events, handling count-valued, directional, and continuous-time series, and the development of unified software resources. Our survey provides both a conceptual framework and a practical roadmap for probabilistic forecasting research.
